P1.evidence: The application was genuinely used, twice and specifically — 'Already saw, of course, the message that you sent, so I already have somewhat of an idea' and later 'You also put in your application because you, of course, just got a newborn. You've been stagnant for like a year now.' The frame ran two of four parts: 'go through what your goals are, where you're currently at, and yeah, see if we can be a part of that, if not, totally fine, I'll point you in the right direction.' No agreement question was asked at all — he went straight from the frame into the open question, which did land cleanly.

P2.evidence: Injury work was the best in the batch: severity scaled 1-10, situational variation established, onset traced to the box squat, progression asked ('is it something that ever since you did that like one and a half years ago, it's been getting worse?'), current treatment established, and a sweep for anything else which surfaced the shoulder. Training week, results and diet all properly asked. But work was never asked — the prospect's occupation is not established anywhere in 57 minutes — and neither were health conditions. Sleep is the costly one: he raised it himself in his first answer ('since I've had my recent daughter, so sleep is just, yeah') and again as the reason sessions collapse ('because of, you know, bad sleep or whatever'), and it was never once picked up on a man with a two-and-a-half-month-old. Energy was never asked either, which is how the lightheadedness only surfaced at 00:40 by accident.

P3.evidence: The surface goals were well drawn out — 'What's like the thing that you feel like is pushing it down the most?' produced the midsection and the arms, and the can't-do question produced the kids and the yard. But the bridge out of the physical was not just missed, it was closed off: 'as it mainly comes down to physical aspects, building more muscle in your upper body, becoming more lean, getting rid of the back pain.' Nobody asked who else this impacts, on a call with four children and a wife in it. The prospect had already handed over the material — 'the goal of getting it repaired and going through all that headache was to play with my kids and be able to mow the yard' — and it was acknowledged and dropped. The consequence of that omission arrives forty minutes later as 'My wife is not dying for me to look great.'

P4.evidence: 'have you tried to sort of change the way that you're currently doing things already before?' opened it and produced the Facebook-protocol pattern in the prospect's own words. 'Is that stagnant in the sense of just not seeing the progress... or is it also just with being very inconsistent?' split the two causes cleanly, and he named the gap himself: 'either I don't know what workouts to do or have someone guiding me there.' The rep also asked the useful competitor question — 'what got you to stop from going to those other people that you've seen come by already?' The scripted 'The information isn't the problem' line never ran, against a prospect whose exact complaint was that he has plenty of information and no structure.

P5.evidence: Both of the first two ran. 'how do you think that that would look like if nothing really changes in the approach that you're currently having?' produced a real answer — 'I've contemplated not going to the gym anymore, right? What's the point if I'm not gaining anything' — and the settle question followed verbatim: 'is that something that you're willing to settle for?' The answer was 'No, that's why I'm reaching out to a coach', and rather than asking why not, the rep spent the next thirty seconds explaining why he had asked the question. No line in the sand. Because the phase stopped at the surface, the cost of inaction on the table was disappointment, not anything that could outweigh $6,000 of a family budget.

P6.evidence: 'Do you think if you can commit to that, that you're actually going to be able to get to your goals?' ran before the presentation and returned 'Yeah. I mean, I'm ready to pull the trigger.' A 1-10 gate followed after the pillars and returned 8-9, and the follow-up was good practice — 'Do you have any more questions to make sure you are at like a 10 level for you?' — which surfaced the load-equivalence doubt. But the gate question itself pre-loaded price as the only remaining variable ('I don't have any questions on it. It just comes down to the investments'), the doubt was answered with an anecdote rather than resolved, and the all-in question was never asked.

P11.evidence: No agreement on either tier, so no payment or onboarding step became reachable. The rep did correctly sequence what would happen — investment, then the Trevor booking, then the onboarding form — before naming the price.

objection_plays.detail: The two best moves ran. The isolate: 'outside of the investment... do you feel like, is this something I would want to do?' And a clean separation of worth from capacity: 'it's more of a, is it worth it at the moment rather than if it's possible? Like that's what I'm hearing, right?' — confirmed by the prospect. Everything after that stopped. No open-conversation ask, no 'most clients pay upfront but for some we break it up', no payment plan mentioned at any point on the call, and not one of the six financial-picture questions. Having correctly diagnosed a worth problem rather than a capacity problem, the rep then solved it by lowering the price rather than by raising the worth.

The wife entered the call as an obstacle and was never worked. 'My wife is not dying for me to look great' and 'as a family, do we think that taking $6,000 out of the budget is something' are the trigger in substance. None of the play ran: he was not asked whether, money aside, he personally felt this could get him there; not asked what obstacles might come up when he raised it with her; and never asked the central question, whether there is any reason she would not want him stronger and out of the back pain that stops him picking up their four children. That last one was available and free, because the back pain had been established in detail forty minutes earlier.

Probing ran and was useful — 'what's it that you're mainly want to think about?' established that the decision was between tiers rather than whether to buy, and 'When do you think that you'll be able to actually have that good think about it?' set a timeline. None of the substantive moves ran. Worth noting in the rep's favour: once a family bereavement was disclosed he stopped pushing entirely and simply exchanged numbers, which was the right call.

Proof of the modality. The prospect's only stated hesitation before price was mechanical and specific: whether a two-handed 35 lb kettlebell can do what 90 lb dumbbells do for a man who already curls 45 lb one-handed. He said plainly 'Just want to see it lived out.' There is no scripted play, no trial, no demonstration and no evidence pack; the answer was a personal anecdote about being more tired than expected. This is a distinct gap from the clinical and cheaper-substitute ones already logged.

Reduced scope. 'I'd rather be more independent and get some check-ins than have constant access that I may or may not use' is not a money objection and Objection C does not reach it. The prospect is asking to buy less of the thing the price is built on. The only available response was to move him to a different product, which is a pricing decision standing in for a packaging one.

notes: Baseline and Past Attempts were strong and the injury history was the most thoroughly gathered in the batch. Two omissions decided it. Phase 3 was closed off at the physical, so when the wife and the family budget arrived at 00:46 there was no emotional stake to weigh against them and no reason for her to want this. And the presentation left out unlimited access to Trevor, which is what the $6,000 is for — the prospect priced it at $500 a month on the information he had been given, and the rep only found out after the number was refused.
